 New Airfare Rules from January 2027: Centre gets powers to intervene, airlines must disclose full ticket costs
 India will adopt the Bharatiya Vayuyan Niyam, 2026, starting January 1, 2027, introducing stricter airfare transparency while retaining government intervention powers for extraordinary situations.
 By   Storyboard18 |  November 2, 2026, 10:08:24 IST Choose Storyboard18 on Follow Share A key provision under Rule 192(6) empowers the Central Government to issue written directions to air transport undertakings if it considers that an extraordinary situation has arisen and intervention is necessary in the public interest. ADVERTISEMENT
 India’s aviation sector is set to operate under a new regulatory framework from January 1, 2027, with the Centre introducing stricter fare disclosure requirements and retaining the authority to intervene in airline pricing during extraordinary situations in the public interest. The Bharatiya Vayuyan Niyam, 2026, notified in the Official Gazette on October 31, does not introduce a standing cap on airfares but establishes provisions for greater tariff transparency and government oversight.
 Under Rule 192, airlines will continue to determine their tariffs, taking into account factors such as operating costs. However, the rules require air transport operators to submit their established tariffs to the Director General of Civil Aviation (DGCA) in the format and at intervals specified by the regulator. Airlines must also publish these tariffs on their websites and other digital platforms in the manner prescribed by the DGCA.
 The rules further mandate that passengers be shown the total amount payable at the time of booking, with the same amount reflected on the ticket. Airlines will have to provide a separate breakdown of the base fare, taxes, fees, cancellation charges, refund conditions and other applicable charges.
 The distinction between taxes and fees has also been specified. While taxes refer to payments made to the government, fees cover payments to service providers for facilities or services extended to passengers. The DGCA will monitor tariffs established by scheduled domestic air transport operators.

 A key provision under Rule 192(6) empowers the Central Government to issue written directions to air transport undertakings if it considers that an extraordinary situation has arisen and intervention is necessary in the public interest.
 However, the provision places certain conditions on such intervention. Any direction issued by the government must be proportionate to the circumstances and remain effective only for the period specified in the direction.
 The notification does not define what constitutes an extraordinary situation or prescribe a numerical threshold for government intervention. It also does not introduce mandatory prior government approval for individual airline fares or a fixed formula for determining ticket prices on routes served by a single airline.
 The framework, therefore, retains the existing market-based approach to fare determination while providing the government with a mechanism to intervene under specified exceptional circumstances.
 Supreme Court proceedings put airfare regulation in focus 
 The notification comes against the backdrop of proceedings in the Supreme Court concerning allegations of arbitrary and excessive airfares. On October 16, Solicitor General Tushar Mehta informed the court that the new rules had received administrative approval and would be published within two weeks. The court subsequently directed the Centre to place the notified rules before it by November 16.
 India has followed a deregulated airfare regime since 1994, when airlines were allowed to determine ticket prices. The Civil Aviation Ministry has maintained that fares are generally governed by market conditions, with airlines using multiple pricing bands depending on demand and the timing of bookings.
 Under the existing Aircraft Rules, 1937, Rule 135(4) also empowered the DGCA to issue directions in cases involving excessive or predatory tariffs or oligopolistic practices. The new Rule 192 retains the regulator's tariff-monitoring responsibility but does not reproduce these specific grounds for DGCA intervention.
 The Bharatiya Vayuyan Niyam, 2026, has been framed under the Bharatiya Vayuyan Adhiniyam, 2024, which replaced the Aircraft Act, 1934. The new rules will replace the Aircraft Rules, 1937, from January 1, 2027, subject to the notification's savings provisions.
